title: Pause
tagline: Designing friction that helps people scroll on purpose.
headline: Downloads went up 149%. So why did people quit in week one?
summary: I built Pause, an iOS app that puts a short puzzle in front of the apps you scroll on autopilot. Solo, with Claude Code as my engineering partner, seven prepaid early users to ask, and analytics to show me where people quit.
outcomes: 9 puzzles on one shared shell at launch, 10+ now, plus seasonal themes
7 early users prepaid and shaped the first versions. Apple Search Ads brought 100-something installs, Reddit brought none
The leak was week one: Day 7 retention is 16%, the target is 30%
lessons: AI made building cheap. Knowing what's right is still the job
Distribution is the only moat that counts
article:
I was spending 9 hours a day on Instagram. Screen Time limits did nothing to reduce that time. The limit sheet always had an "Ignore Limit" button, and one tap put me right back in the feed. Low friction, easy to bypass.

So I built Pause. It puts a short brainteaser in front of the apps I choose. Solve the puzzle and I'm in. I can still scroll, but I do it when I truly decide.

Those daily 9 hours went down to one. I knew this was a problem a lot of people had, but having proof made me more confident going to the market.

I designed it, built it with Claude Code as my engineering partner, and shipped it. I started in July and had a first version out by the first week of August. My first users were friends and family, and they shaped the first versions. When social didn't move the needle, I put $1,000 into ads (Reddit and App Store Ads), only to find out people were dropping in week one. This is how it went, what I got wrong, and what I'm changing in the next version.

**Tools:** Figma, Claude Code, PostHog, App Store Connect, Applyra

## 1. The problem

Screen Time limits work right up until you need them. The pull is strongest exactly when you're worst at holding your own line, and the way out is one tap away. I knew I was doomscrolling and I did it anyway.

![One tap to bypass: the iOS Time Limit screen](content/pause/easy-to-bypass.jpg)

I also saw a gap in the market. I looked at apps like ClearSpace, Forest and One Sec, among others. They were either too restrictive or too easy to bypass.

The question I kept coming back to:

> How much friction is enough to break autopilot, without making people feel punished or locked out of their own phone?

Too little and it's a toothless timer. Too much and people delete the app.

## 2. The first call: block it or slow it down

The obvious version of a screen time app is a hard block: a timer that locks the app until it runs out. It's strong, but it feels like punishment, and per secondary research, people are likely to delete apps that punish them.

I went with a quick puzzle instead. It's enough to interrupt autopilot without locking anyone out. Opening Instagram becomes a choice you make, not a reflex.

## 3. Designing the happy path

I started in Figma with the happy path: what the app looks like when everything goes right. Before any code existed, I picked the colors, the brand and the theme.

![The original happy path, designed in Figma](content/pause/original-happy-path.jpg)

Three rules guided it:

1. **A pause, not a punishment.** Warm gradients, soft glass and calm copy. No red warning screens.
2. **One shell, many games.** The puzzles change and everything around them stays the same, so you learn it once.
3. **Don't collect what I don't need.** Analytics are counts only. Which apps you block and anything you type stay on your phone.

![Every puzzle in the same shell](content/pause/all-puzzles-same-shell.jpg)

I launched with 9 puzzles. The shared shell is why the app doesn't turn into a mess, but more on that later.

## 4. Building it with Claude Code

Once the happy path was ready, I sent it to Claude Code and we built it in Xcode. I own the problem, the taste and what ships. Claude turns my Figma frames into SwiftUI, reviews the code for risk, tech debt and drift from the style guide, sets up the analytics in PostHog and checks that builds pass.

The happy path was the easy part. The missing cases showed up when I tested on my phone. I'd find something that wasn't there, take a screenshot, annotate it in Figma, and tell Claude Code to go back to the frame and check the style guide. Then we'd go around again.

The loop:

1. **Design it in Figma first.** Claude reads the exact frame through the Figma MCP, so nothing gets rebuilt from my memory of it.
2. **One thing at a time.** One puzzle, one screen, one detail per pass, so my review stays sharp.
3. **Test on my phone/simulator.** I find what's missing, annotate the screenshot in Figma and send Claude back to the frame. I make the call on how it feels.
4. **Write the decision down,** so the next session starts with context instead of a re-explanation.

![Working alongside the simulator, with design feedback](content/pause/emulator-and-design-feedback.jpg)

AI made it cheap to act on my judgment. It didn't replace it. The question used to be whether I could build something. Now it's whether I know what's worth building and can tell when it's right, and that's still the design job.

## 5. My first users

My first users were friends and family. I shared the idea with a few of them, and 7 decided to prepay $20 each. For that, they got the first version and a full year of service. It was a deep discount since the price started at $75 a year. Eventually I lowered it to $50 after early market responses.

The money mattered less than what it gave me: a group I could ask. When I was stuck on a decision, I could put it to them. Which puzzle do you prefer, this one or that one? What feature should I work on next? That early feedback was critical in shaping what became the first published version.

![A poll in my early users' WhatsApp group: matching puzzles to specific apps got the most votes](content/pause/whatsapp-poll.jpg)

Matching puzzles to specific apps got the most votes. Timed options came next, tied with a free trial that doesn't require a credit card and a 3 month plan.

Three ideas came out of that group, and all three are in the app:

- **Timing sessions:** different time limits for when you open an app
- **Difficulty per app:** the apps that pull hardest get a harder puzzle
- **A view of your time:** how your time has been spent and how many times you walked away from the scroll

More importantly, the group validated the idea. They talk about it in gatherings, they tell me they love it because it helps them control their screen time.

Side note: I didn't see this coming, but users keep telling me they love the puzzles. Some just open Pause to play the games for a bit.

![Friction per app: an idea from my first users](content/pause/puzzle-difficulty.jpg)

## 6. Going wide

Once I had the group, I got louder about it on Instagram, LinkedIn and Threads. About 20 users came from there so it wasn't moving the needle.

I'm also focused on App Store Optimization (ASO). Using Applyra, a tool that aggregates App Store data, I designed the first strategy around the app's title, subtitle and keywords, the main ingredients of ranking in the store.

During the first two months I kept tweaking these values to see if I would rank higher, but nothing seemed to work.

![Applyra: keyword ranks stayed flat](content/pause/applyra.jpg)

So I put $1,000 into ads, split evenly between Reddit and Apple Search Ads. Reddit brought 0 installs. Apple brought all of the 100-something installs I tested.

### Downloads went up, but conversion rate went down

Before the ads (August 31) and after (October 1). I ran ads on most days of September.

| Metric | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Impressions | 2.19k | 23.7k | +982% |
| Product page views | 364 | 924 | +154% |
| Conversion rate | 6.07% | 1.38% |  -77% |
| First-time downloads | 81 | 202 | +149% |

![App Store Connect: acquisition, the latest view (newer than the dates in the table)](content/pause/appstore-connect-data.jpg)

## 7. What the data showed

The installs were real. PostHog showed where those people stopped:

- If you denied Screen Time or Notifications, you got stuck. Screen Time had no way back, because iOS doesn't put a Screen Time switch on the app's Settings page.
- A lot of people dropped at app selection, the app system picker had no context or additional helper text
- Free users got stuck on the only puzzle they had.

I had planned the free version as a way in. Free users would see ads, get access to just one puzzle, and be able to block only 3 apps. My hypothesis was that those limits would be enough to push people toward premium, with all the puzzles and a lot more features. The data said otherwise. Free users didn't convert, and a lot of people never made it past setup.

### Missing gaps

Through PostHog data, I learned that free users were getting stuck on the only available puzzle, Word Jumble. Get the word wrong and there was no way out, right when they were already annoyed, so the puzzle added more friction than people were looking for, and they dropped, completely.

![PostHog: the Word Jumble funnel](content/pause/mvql5muo-screenshot-2026-10-27-at-6.11.40-am.jpg)

### The real problem was week one

The paid installs made the math clear. It cost about $4.33 to get an install, and each download was worth about $1.14, so every paid install lost about $3. Reddit's $500 brought nothing. Paying subscribers were still in single digits. Buying more installs would only lose more money.

Marketing wasn't the leak. Week one was.

The number I watch now is Day 7 retention: people who open a puzzle 7 or more days after their first one.

![PostHog: weekly retention by cohort](content/pause/posthog-roadmap.jpg)

## 8. What I changed

### Onboarding

Onboarding is where my idea of the flow and what people actually got through were furthest apart. Here's what I changed:

- A "Try Again" button after a denied permission, and "Open Settings" where iOS allows it
- A Choose Apps screen before the picker: "Pick the apps that take up your screen time. Pause steps in before you open them."
- A shorter order: a primer, Screen Time (Step 1 of 2), Notifications (Step 2 of 2), then app selection
- A "Heads up" box that explains why Screen Time access matters before iOS asks

![The new onboarding](content/pause/mvqlboxq-screenshot-2026-10-27-at-6.16.29-am.jpg)

### Word Jumble

The same puzzle that trapped people now gives them a way out:

- Added a retry button
- Added a "Show word" button that appears after a few wrong answers
- Anagrams count as correct
- A "Mix letters" button to shuffle

![Word Jumble after the fixes, with Mix letters and Show word](content/pause/mvqlktxv-screenshot-2026-10-27-at-6.22.49-am.jpg)

### Trial first

During the first round of ads, I had made the option to continue with a free version upfront during sign-up. Testing and secondary research show that people who use a free version rarely convert.

So for the second test run, I'm still keeping a free version of the app, but only after the free trial has passed and the user hasn't subscribed.

Because of this, switching to trial first meant "No credit card" wasn't true anymore. It was in the Figma hero pills, the screenshot headlines and the end card of the preview video. Claude flagged it before I did, and I changed every one to "7 days free · Cancel anytime."

The new flow uses a trial first model: 7 days free, a reminder on day 5 (two days before it renews) that I disclose during the notifications step, and a free tier after the trial ends.

### Cleaning up the data

I asked Claude to check my analytics and it found I was tracking the wrong things. `puzzle_reset` meant someone tapped Reset, not that they got the answer wrong. `upgraded_to_premium` fired when someone started a trial and never on a real payment. I would've planned the roadmap on bad data.

So I cleaned it up:

- An `is_internal` flag so my own testing doesn't count, and a `first_launch` property
- Subscription events that come from StoreKit instead of guesses in the app
- Onboarding session replay with text, images and the app picker masked, and an updated privacy policy and App Privacy label before it shipped

## 9. What's next: version 1.7

Version 1.7, out Nov 1, is the test. Here's what changes:

- **Trial first.** During onboarding, people start a free trial to try Pause. If they don't subscribe afterward, they fall to the free version.
- **A different free version.** Before, free meant one puzzle, Word Jumble, on up to three apps. Now it's three puzzles on one app, so people see more of the variety. I want to learn whether variety is a better reason to stay than blocking more apps.
- **The Word Jumble fixes,** so nobody hits that dead end again.

The free version still shows ads, through a Google AdMob account. I hope it monetizes once there's real volume.

Before launch I wrote down what a win looks like, so I can't explain the result away afterward. The question is whether these changes move Day 7 retention. I'll update this with the numbers, even if they barely move.

## 10. What I'm learning

- **Telling Claude Code what I want gets better with practice.** I'm getting a lot better at giving instructions and describing exactly what I want to see.
- **Marketing is its own skill.** I'm learning how to get the app in front of people.
- **Feedback only counts if I act on it.** I'm learning how to receive it and how to implement it.

And what I'd tell another designer:

- **Measure from the get go.**
- **One system beats ten screens.** The shell is why 10+ puzzles still feel like one app.
- **Measure what you design.** Without onboarding data I'd still think marketing was the problem.
- **Stop when the data says stop.** The keywords didn't move, so I moved on.
- **AI made building cheap.** Knowing what's right is still the job.
- **Most importantly:** Distribution is THE only moat that counts and you cannot "vibe marketing"

## Deep dives

### One shell for every puzzle

I started with Word Jumble and kept at it until it felt right. Then I wrote down what made it work and made that the rule for every puzzle after it:

- A blue to warm amber gradient with a faint scribble texture
- A top bar with the puzzle name and a close button
- A Young Serif title at 24pt with a quiet subtitle like "Round 1 of 3"
- 56×56 glass tiles with a 4pt radius, and a dark overlay on the active one

Only the game area changes. That's why Sixdoku makes sense in a few seconds even the first time you see it. I launched with 9 puzzles, and Memory Match was the first addition, at Halloween.

### Seasonal themes

I wanted the app to feel alive and give people an opportunity to resonate with the season, so I decided to celebrate each upcoming season (Halloween, Thanksgiving, and Christmas).

So I built a SeasonalTheme system (gradients, accent colors, fonts and decor) that resolves once on launch.

- **Halloween:** purple gradients, the Metal Mania display font, a moon, bats and webs, a new splash and puzzle thumbnails, and a Memory Match puzzle with a seasonal deck.
- **Thanksgiving:** a new theme and app icon, an embossed splash wordmark, and a Gratitude puzzle.
- **Christmas:** TBD at the time of this writing (October 2026)

![The dashboard in its default, Halloween and Thanksgiving themes](content/pause/apps-season-theme.jpg)

Gratitude asks for three things you're grateful for, each at least 5 characters and all different. The answers stay on your phone, and later reminders quote one back to you. Analytics only log that you finished, never what you wrote. It's the puzzle where the pause is supposed to feel good.

A few rules kept it consistent: text on the gradient is white, cards keep dark text, and the code is the source of truth.

### Beyond the app

I also own everything that gets people to the app:

- **try-pause.com,** designed and built from scratch, initially built on Webflow but eventually hosted on GitHub Pages to save on cost. It's written in first person ("I built") on purpose. It's one person, and I didn't want it to pretend to be a team.
- **The App Store listing:** screenshot sets and a preview video for each seasonal release, plus keyword research.
- **SEO:** GA4 and Search Console, a canonical fix, an internal-linking pass, and blog posts comparing Pause with other screen time apps.
- **A public roadmap** where people vote on what I build next.

![try-pause.com in its Halloween theme](content/pause/marketing-site-halloween.jpg)

![The public roadmap, with votes](content/pause/public-roadmap-votes.jpg)

### To the Future and Beyond

I'm having a lot of fun building Pause and thinking of ways to delight my users and maintain the app.

I'm NOT having as much fun marketing it and trying to bring people in, which is considerably harder in this day and time.

But whether this tiny endeavor becomes successful or not, the skills I've learned here make me feel like I have super powers. With Claude Code as an engineering partner, we could build almost anything.

beats.question: Kill or keep the Mini Crossword?

optionA.label: Mini Crossword
optionA.body: Same clue every time, no hints. A real one needs a fill algorithm and a clue database. More complexity than a v1 needs.

optionB.label: Word Search
optionB.body: A fresh 8×8 board every time from a list of calm words. No timer, no way to fail.

beats.why: The gate shows up many times a day. A puzzle that repeats is worse than no puzzle.
